newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain to try to cement French support for EMU bid.
newsitem.headline: Spain to try to cement French support for EMU bid.

text.p: Spain will try to cement French support on Monday for it to take part in the launch of Europe's single currency and overcome doubts about its fitness to join the continent's economic powers.

Spanish Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato will put forward his nation's dramatic economic improvement to ensure France, seen as a core founding member of the euro with Germany, will back Spain's candidacy.

The regular twice yearly meeting of French and Spanish finance ministers will focus on the two nations' economic progress and European Monetary and Economic Union, and the follow-up to a European Union summit in Dublin in December which laid the groundwork for the practical running of monetary union.

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis is likely to be sympathetic to Spain's cause, after French President Jacques Chirac portrayed Spain as a credible contender for the launch at a summit in Madrid last November.

But since then, a top German official and banker have raised serious reservations about Spain's long-term fitness, although Spain itself has fulfilled an additional two of the five Maastricht Treaty economic criteria for the launch.

In February, German Finance Secretary Juergen Stark said some countries did not have the economic track record to join in the euro launch. Although he named no names, market participants believed he was referring to Italy, Spain and Portugal.
But Spain has pressed its economic clean-up project and by early March, data showed it had tentatively achieved inflation levels that met the requirements.

Under the Treaty, inflation may not exceed the average of the three best EU performers by more than 1.5 points in 1997. In February, Spain's year-on-year rate slid to 2.5 percent from 2.9 percent in January and 3.7 in February 1996.
It also met the currency stability criteria in early March, having held its currency stable for two years since its last devaluation on March 8, 1995.
The Maastricht Treaty lays down economic targets on inflation, interest and exchange rates, budget deficits and public debt which nations must meet this year to join the euro from the start.
Spain fulfils long-term interest rate rules in addition to inflation and currency stability. It is also considered to be on schedule for deficit and debt criteria.
Given its increasing economic progress, German scepticism has angered Spain and it will be looking for assurances that France remains in its camp.
"There is no doubt we will be able to fulfil the criteria," Rato told Reuters earlier this week.
"Some people in Europe should not be speaking about other countries. They should be concentrating on (their own). That is what we are doing," Rato said.
France is likely to be receptive.

"France will look to support the Mediterranean countries for competitive reasons and to have a political balance to counter the extreme strength of the core (nations to the north), said Xavier Secura Porta, chief of research at Caja de Cataluna.
